idiom_name: tokio TcpStream + tokio-util Framed/LengthDelimitedCodec with serde-derived messages
implementation_notes: Rust splits the two halves cleanly: tokio provides the transport and tokio-util's Framed with LengthDelimitedCodec turns a TcpStream into a stream and sink of whole frames (a big-endian u32 length header, configurable through LengthDelimitedCodec::builder()), so the forwarder is frames.send(bytes) and the receiver is a while-let over frames.next(); serde (or bincode/prost) performs the marshal/unmarshal and a match on a message enum dispatches to the peer method. Ownership means the roles are values moved into the tasks that use them, so there is no shared mutable forwarder to synchronise; the classic hand-written envelope and reader-thread pair is justified only when the framing must match an existing non-Rust peer byte for byte. tarpc or tonic replace both halves with generated stubs when a schema-driven RPC is acceptable.
pitfalls: LengthDelimitedCodec defaults to an 8 MiB maximum frame and turns anything larger into an io error - a deliberate bound that must be chosen consciously.
bincode/prost are not self-describing, so a decoder built from a different schema version mis-decodes silently; keep an explicit version field in the envelope.
A sink that is dropped (or a send whose flush is never awaited) loses buffered frames - close the stream explicitly and handle the final error.
